claims.reason: The passage states verbatim that Carnival is the largest global cruise company, among the largest leisure travel companies, with the exact list of cruise lines cited.
All four figures in the claim (LTM revenue $27.6B, LTM EBITDA $7.3B, FY0 revenue $26.6B, FY0 EBITDA $7.3B) match the metric values computed from XBRL data.
The passage states each brand meets a distinct set of consumer psychographics/vacation needs, allowing penetration of large addressable customer segments, matching the claim.
The filing explicitly states ship mobility allows redeploying vessels between regions to meet changing demand, matching the claim, though it does not explicitly mention cash flows.
The passage confirms travel agents are integral to distribution and that no group of agencies under common control accounted for 10% or more of revenues.

The passage supports competition risk against cruise and land-based vacations affecting sales, pricing and destination options, but the evidence describes 'overcapacity and competition,' not 'capacity-constrained,' which the claim asserts.
All four leverage values match the computed metric scorecard exactly.
All four metric values match the scorecard exactly.

The debt figures ($26.6B at FY0 and $23.9B at LTM) match the computed metric values, but the evidence includes no leverage metric data to support the claim that this caused an improvement in leverage metrics.
The passage states net income rose from $2.3 billion in 2025 to $2.7 billion in 2026 for the nine-month year-to-date period.
Evidence shows large capex ($2.1B over nine months) primarily on ship improvements, new shipbuilding and exclusive destinations, a substantial use of cash.
The passage describes debt transactions involving refinancing, modification and extinguishment of existing debt, and associated extinguishment/modification costs.
Both liquidity coverage values match the metric values computed from XBRL data: 1.42x for the twelve months to 31 August 2026 and 1.31x for FY ended 30 November 2025.
CFO, capex, and short-term debt figures match the metric values, but dividends of $0 and short-term investments of $0 are assumptions ('assumed zero: not reported'), not reported facts.
Both the $4.5 billion available under the multicurrency revolving credit facility and $1.2 billion cash as of August 31, 2026 are stated in the passage and consistent with the metric value.
The passage states the revolving facility may be drawn through June 2030 subject to satisfaction of conditions.
The passage directly states undrawn export credit facilities fund ship deliveries planned through 2033.

The passage directly states the $9.1 billion working capital deficit as of August 31, 2026 and attributes it to customer deposits collected ahead of sailings, used with other cash to fund operations, service debt and support capital investments.
All six figures in the claim match the computed debt maturity values for FY2025.

All figures (debt due within 24 months of $5.1 billion, 19.2% share, total debt of $26.6 billion at FY ended 30 Nov 2025) match the computed metrics, and the remainder being spread across later years follows by difference.

All figures in the claim (cover of 2.66x, cash of $1.9B, short-term debt of $2.6B, undrawn revolver of $0) match the FY0 metric values computed from the XBRL data, including the zero assumptions for short-term investments and undrawn revolver.
The passage directly states the repricing and prepayment of the 2027 and 2028 term loan facilities, new senior unsecured note issuances, and prepayments of other debt instruments during 2025.
The evidence states prepayments of $11.6 billion occurred and $409 million of debt extinguishment and modification costs were recognized in the income statement during 2025.

The evidence explicitly states compliance with covenants at August 31, 2026, lists a minimum liquidity covenant, and confirms cross-default/cross-acceleration clauses could make substantially all outstanding debt due on default.
All parts of the claim are directly stated in the passage.
The claim directly restates the risk factor passage listing pandemics, inflation, higher interest rates and other general concerns leading to decline in cruise demand and negative impacts.
The passage directly states fuel volatility can lead to increased fuel costs and reduced profitability.

The passage explicitly states cybersecurity incidents have led to and may continue to lead to disruptions in business operations, financial losses, regulatory fines and penalties, and reputational damage.
The metrics confirm SB-4 grade, weighted score 3.95, non-provisional status with all six factors scored, and that it is a stylized scorecard grade rather than a credit rating.
Interest coverage (EBITDA/interest) has the best (lowest) band of all six factors at band 3 with weight 25.0% and an LTM value of 6.21x; all other factors score band 4 or 6.
All stated bands and weights match the metric values exactly.
The metric value (2.66x), band 6 (weakest among factors, since all others are band 4 or better), and 10.0% weight all match the evidence.

Capex of $2.1B being a substantial cash use is supported, but the evidence shows no deleveraging improvement or improved coverage (interest coverage is a middle band 3, and no trend data is given), so those parts go beyond the evidence.
The passage confirms both a substantial working capital deficit and cross-default provisions that could make substantially all debt due on an event of default.
